planting.note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings in spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil, including caliche and limestone sites most other grape species reject.

directions: Champin's grape is a wild Texas species valued far more as a rootstock and breeding parent than as a table fruit, best known for lending its extreme drought and Pierce's disease tolerance to hybrids like 'Champanel.' Its small, tart, thick-skinned black fruit is edible but rarely grown for direct eating. Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun; it thrives on poor, rocky, alkaline soils, including limestone and caliche, where other grape species struggle. Once established it is exceptionally tough and drought tolerant, needing minimal irrigation beyond its first season.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil, sheltering young plants from hard frost until established.

directions: Kohuhu is the New Zealand wild-type species behind the many variegated and purple-leaved garden selections already sold, bearing glossy, wavy-margined leaves on a dense, fast-growing evergreen shrub or small tree. Tiny, intensely fragrant dark purple flowers open in spring, more noticeable by scent than appearance. Grow it in partial sun on well-drained soil, sheltered from the hardest frosts and strong drying winds in its first few years. It takes well to hedging and screening and tolerates coastal salt exposure once established.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring into well-drained soil with room to develop its eventual broad, picturesque form.

directions: Japanese white pine is the species behind the many dwarf and tightly needled bonsai and garden cultivars already grown, carrying soft, bluish-green needles in bundles of five on a slow, broadly conical to irregular tree. In cultivation it is prized for its graceful, often windswept-looking silhouette and tidy, fine-textured foliage. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and avoid wet, heavy clay, which predisposes it to root problems. It grows slowly and tolerates shaping well, making it equally suited to a specimen tree role or careful pruning into a more compact garden form.

planting.note: Divide and repot in spring into a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping the plant in warm, humid, bright-indirect conditions year-round.

directions: Rose-painted calathea is the Brazilian wild-type species behind the many named patterned-leaf houseplant cultivars already sold, with broad, dark green leaves marked by a rose-pink to cream midrib stripe and a wine-purple underside. Like its cultivars it is grown almost entirely as a houseplant in temperate climates, demanding warm temperatures, high humidity, and protection from direct sun and cold drafts. Pot in a well-drained, peat-based mix and keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, since both dry air and soggy roots cause rapid decline. Its leaves rise and fold at night in the classic prayer-plant fashion, a sign of a healthy, contented plant.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in deep shade.

directions: Takao wild ginger is the Japanese wild-type species behind the several silver-patterned named cultivars already grown as collector shade groundcovers, carrying heart-shaped evergreen leaves with a naturally mottled silvery overlay that varies from plant to plant in the wild. It spreads slowly into a low, dense colony in the deep shade of a woodland garden, where its hidden maroon flowers at soil level go largely unnoticed except by close inspection. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade, protected from direct sun and wind that can scorch the leaves. It is slow-growing and best left undisturbed once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into moist, well-drained soil; give it room, since the wild species grows larger than most named garden selections.

directions: Sargent viburnum is the East Asian wild-type species behind the compact, red-berried garden selections already grown, forming a large, rounded multi-stemmed shrub with maple-like lobed leaves and flat clusters of white spring flowers. Showy red fruit ripens in fall and often persists into winter, providing food for birds after most other berries are gone. Plant in full sun to light shade on moist, well-drained soil, and give it generous room since the wild species grows considerably larger than the compact cultivars bred from it. It tolerates cold, heat, and a range of soils well once established, needing little more than an occasional thinning of old wood.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring into well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Downy lilac is the Chinese wild-type species behind the compact, mildew-resistant named selections such as 'Miss Kim,' bearing fragrant lavender-pink flower panicles and leaves with a soft, downy underside. It blooms slightly later than common lilac, extending the lilac season, and grows into a broad, rounded shrub somewhat larger than its well-known garden cultivars. Plant in full sun on well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil, and prune immediately after flowering to maintain shape without sacrificing next year's buds. It tolerates cold and heat well and is notably more resistant to powdery mildew than common lilac.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide and repot in spring into a well-drained, peaty mix, keeping the plant warm, humid, and out of direct sun.

directions: Stromanthe is the Brazilian wild-type species behind the popular variegated 'Triostar' and related houseplant selections, bearing long, glossy, dark green lance-shaped leaves with a vivid magenta-red underside. In its plain wild form the leaf color is solid rather than splashed with cream variegation, but the plant shares the same demand for warmth, high humidity, and bright, indirect light. Pot in a well-drained, peat-based mix and keep soil consistently moist, using filtered or distilled water where possible, since it is sensitive to mineral buildup and chlorinated tap water. Protect it from cold drafts and direct afternoon sun, both of which quickly scorch or curl the foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rooted canes in spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil, and site it where its vigorous, thorny growth can be contained, since it spreads readily and can naturalize in mild, wet climates.

directions: Cutleaf blackberry is the European wild-type species behind the thornless 'Evergreen' and 'Oregon Thornless' selections already grown, identified by its deeply cut, almost fern-like leaflets on vigorous, thorny trailing canes. It produces abundant, flavorful black fruit in mid to late summer but is noticeably more aggressive and thorny than its thornless garden derivatives, and has naturalized as a weed in parts of the Pacific Northwest. Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun on well-drained soil, and prune and train canes attentively to keep this vigorous grower within bounds. Given its tendency to spread by root and cane tip, site it away from wild areas where it could escape cultivation.

common_name: European Ground Cherry (Mongolian Cherry, Wild-Type Species)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring into well-drained soil; it suckers to form a low thicket, so give it room or plan to contain the spread.

directions: European ground cherry, also called Mongolian cherry, is the extremely cold-hardy Eurasian wild-type species used as a breeding parent behind several bush-cherry hybrids already grown for fruit in harsh northern climates. The species itself is a low, suckering, thicket-forming shrub bearing small, tart red cherries useful for preserves and juice rather than fresh eating. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; it tolerates extreme winter cold and poor soils far better than standard sweet or sour cherry trees. Left unchecked it spreads by root suckers into a dense colony, so gardeners wanting a single specimen should remove suckers regularly.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or small plugs after frost danger passes into well-drained soil, and shear lightly through the season to maintain bushiness.

directions: Nemesia fruticans is the South African wild-type species behind the many named mounding and trailing bedding cultivars already grown, bearing small, two-lipped flowers in shades of white, lavender, and blue over a long bloom season. Unlike the showier hybrid bedding types, the species itself tends toward smaller, more subdued flowers but shares the same tidy, bushy habit and pleasant fragrance in some forms. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, and provide afternoon shade in hot summer climates to extend bloom and reduce heat stress. Regular light shearing keeps plants compact and encourages a continuous flush of new flowers.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Mahonia eurybracteata is the Chinese wild-type species behind the popular soft, non-spiny 'Soft Caress'-type garden selections, carrying narrow, finely toothed evergreen leaflets with a fern-like texture unlike the stiff, spiky foliage of most mahonias. Fragrant clusters of small yellow flowers open in late fall and winter, drawing pollinators when little else is in bloom, followed by blue-black berries favored by birds. Plant in partial to full shade on moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, where it tolerates the dry shade beneath trees better than many broadleaf evergreens. It needs little pruning beyond removing the occasional leggy stem to keep a tidy, mounded form.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist to wet soil in partial sun, such as a pond margin or rain garden.

directions: Tufted sedge is the European wild-type species behind the golden-leaved 'Bowles Golden' and similar named selections, forming dense, upright tussocks of narrow leaves in boggy meadows, streambanks, and pond margins. In its plain green form it is a durable, clump-forming wetland sedge well suited to naturalizing at the edge of water features. Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in partial sun to light shade, where it tolerates both shallow standing water and periods of more typical garden moisture. Established clumps need little care beyond an occasional tidy-up of old foliage in late winter.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in partial sun; this straight species is less commonly offered than its Korean variety (var. insularis) but shares the same easy care.

directions: Chinese boxwood is the mainland Chinese wild-type species in the same complex that gave rise to the cold-hardy Korean boxwood variety already common in gardens, sharing small, glossy evergreen leaves and a dense, easily shaped habit. It is slower growing than common boxwood but notably resistant to boxwood blight and leafminer pressure that affects some other species. Plant in partial sun to light shade on well-drained soil, and avoid waterlogged sites, which predispose boxwood roots to rot. It takes well to shearing into hedges or formal shapes, or can be left to grow into a naturally rounded specimen shrub.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from harsh winter exposure.

directions: Noble wild ginger is the Japanese wild-type species behind striking patterned-leaf collector selections such as 'Iron Butterfly' and 'Netscape,' bearing rounded evergreen leaves marked with a bold, dark-green and silver mottled pattern unique to each plant. It grows slowly into a low, dense colony in the dappled shade of a woodland garden, with inconspicuous maroon flowers hidden at soil level beneath the foliage. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, with some winter protection in the colder end of its hardiness range. It resents root disturbance once established, so site it thoughtfully from the start.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
